answer.title: How to Evaluate a Stock: A Source-Grounded Framework
sections: Buffett describes selecting equities in the same way one would evaluate a business for acquisition in its entirety: it must be a business you can understand, with favorable long-term prospects, operated by honest and competent people, and available at an attractive price. He notes that market conditions and Berkshire's size led him to relax the fourth criterion from "a very attractive price" to simply "an attractive price". [[P01-001]]
Use Discounted Future Cash Flows, Not Ratios

The underlying formula is John Burr Williams's: the value of any asset today equals the cash inflows and outflows, discounted at an appropriate rate, that can be expected during the asset's remaining life. The critical difficulty with equities is that the analyst must estimate future "coupons" himself, and management quality can dramatically affect those estimates. Low price-to-book, low P/E, or high dividend yield are far from determinative of whether one is truly buying at value. The cheapest asset by discounted-cash calculation should be purchased regardless of whether it grows, whether its earnings are volatile, or whether its price relative to book and earnings appears high or low. [[P01-008]] [[P01-005]] [[P01-009]]
Calculate Owner Earnings, Not GAAP Earnings or Wall Street Cash Flow

Owner earnings equal reported earnings plus depreciation, depletion, amortization and certain other non-cash charges, less the average annual capitalized expenditures required to maintain long-term competitive position and unit volume. If additional working capital is needed to maintain that position, the increment also belongs in the deduction; however, LIFO-following businesses usually do not require additional working capital if unit volume is unchanged. Buffett stresses that component (c) must be a guess, and he prefers being "vaguely right than precisely wrong." Wall Street "cash flow" figures that add back non-cash charges without subtracting maintenance capital are deceptive, because in manufacturing, retailing, extractive and utility businesses the maintenance requirement is always significant over five to ten years. [[P17-002]] [[P17-003]] [[P17-007]] [[P17-008]]
Judge Growth by Incremental Returns on Capital

Growth is always a component in the calculation of value, and its impact can be negative. Growth benefits investors only when each incremental dollar of capital creates more than a dollar of long-term market value. In a low-return business requiring additional funds, growth destroys value. The best business to own over an extended period employs large amounts of incremental capital at very high rates of return; the worst does the opposite. Most high-return businesses need relatively little capital, so shareholders benefit if such a business pays out earnings in dividends or repurchases stock. [[P01-003]] [[P01-007]] [[P01-010]]

An economic franchise arises from a product or service that is needed or desired, is thought by customers to have no close substitute, and is not subject to price regulation. A franchise can tolerate mismanagement without mortal damage. An ordinary business earns exceptional profits only as the low-cost operator or when supply is tight, and poor management can kill it. Buffett notes that many operations fall in a middle ground between the two classes. The See's Candy example illustrates franchise economics: over twenty years profits grew from $4.2 million to $42.4 million pre-tax while the business required only $18 million of reinvested earnings beyond its initial $7 million net worth, distributing the remaining $410 million in pre-tax profits. [[P19-004]] [[P19-005]] [[P19-003]] [[P16-003]] [[P16-004]]
Stay Within Your Circle and Insist on Margin of Safety

Berkshire attempts to address estimation uncertainty in two ways: first, sticking to businesses believed to be simple and stable in character, because complex or rapidly changing businesses cannot be reliably predicted; second, insisting on a margin of safety in the purchase price. If calculated value is only slightly above market price, the stock is not bought. [[P01-011]] [[P01-012]]

P01-001.label: Valuation, knowability and margin of safety · berkshire-letter-1992:u0074
P01-001.context_title: Valuation, knowability and margin of safety

paragraphs.speaker: Warren Buffett
paragraphs.speaker_basis: Signed shareholder-letter authorship; embedded quotations retain their original introduction.

P01-001.excerpt: Our equity-investing strategy remains little changed from what it was fifteen years ago, when we said in the 1977 annual report: "We select our marketable equity securities in much the way we would evaluate a business for acquisition in its entirety. We want the business to be one (a) that we can understand; (b) with favorable long-term prospects; (c) operated by honest and competent people; and (d) available at a very attractive price." We have seen cause to make only one change in this creed: Because of both market conditions and our size, we now substitute "an attractive price" for "a very attractive price."

P01-008.label: Valuation, knowability and margin of safety · berkshire-letter-1992:u0081
P01-008.context_title: Valuation, knowability and margin of safety

paragraphs.speaker: Warren Buffett
paragraphs.speaker_basis: Signed shareholder-letter authorship; embedded quotations retain their original introduction.

P01-008.excerpt: In The Theory of Investment Value, written over 50 years ago, John Burr Williams set forth the equation for value, which we condense here: The value of any stock, bond or business today is determined by the cash inflows and outflows - discounted at an appropriate interest rate - that can be expected to occur during the remaining life of the asset. Note that the formula is the same for stocks as for bonds. Even so, there is an important, and difficult to deal with, difference between the two: A bond has a coupon and maturity date that define future cash flows; but in the case of equities, the investment analyst must himself estimate the future "coupons." Furthermore, the quality of management affects the bond coupon only rarely - chiefly when management is so inept or dishonest that payment of interest is suspended. In contrast, the ability of management can dramatically affect the equity "coupons."

P01-005.label: Valuation, knowability and margin of safety · berkshire-letter-1992:u0078
P01-005.context_title: Valuation, knowability and margin of safety

paragraphs.speaker: Warren Buffett
paragraphs.speaker_basis: Signed shareholder-letter authorship; embedded quotations retain their original introduction.

P01-005.excerpt: Whether appropriate or not, the term "value investing" is widely used. Typically, it connotes the purchase of stocks having attributes such as a low ratio of price to book value, a low price- earnings ratio, or a high dividend yield. Unfortunately, such characteristics, even if they appear in combination, are far from determinative as to whether an investor is indeed buying something for what it is worth and is therefore truly operating on the principle of obtaining value in his investments. Correspondingly, opposite characteristics - a high ratio of price to book value, a high price-earnings ratio, and a low dividend yield - are in no way inconsistent with a "value" purchase.

P01-009.label: Valuation, knowability and margin of safety · berkshire-letter-1992:u0082
P01-009.context_title: Valuation, knowability and margin of safety

paragraphs.speaker: Warren Buffett
paragraphs.speaker_basis: Signed shareholder-letter authorship; embedded quotations retain their original introduction.

P01-009.excerpt: The investment shown by the discounted-flows-of-cash calculation to be the cheapest is the one that the investor should purchase - irrespective of whether the business grows or doesn't, displays volatility or smoothness in its earnings, or carries a high price or low in relation to its current earnings and book value. Moreover, though the value equation has usually shown equities to be cheaper than bonds, that result is not inevitable: When bonds are calculated to be the more attractive investment, they should be bought.

P17-002.label: Owner earnings: full concluding discussion and qualifications · berkshire-letter-1986:u0286
P17-002.context_title: Owner earnings: full concluding discussion and qualifications
P17-002.date_basis: Signature date recorded in the reviewed original-source dossier; report year is separate.

paragraphs.speaker: Warren Buffett
paragraphs.speaker_basis: Signed shareholder-letter authorship; embedded quotations retain their original introduction.

P17-002.excerpt: If we think through these questions, we can gain some insights about what may be called "owner earnings." These represent (a) reported earnings plus (b) depreciation, depletion, amortization, and certain other non-cash charges such as Company N's items (1) and (4) less ( c) the average annual amount of capitalized expenditures for plant and equipment, etc. that the business requires to fully maintain its long-term competitive position and its unit volume. (If the business requires additional working capital to maintain its competitive position and unit volume, the increment also should be included in ( c) . However, businesses following the LIFO inventory method usually do not require additional working capital if unit volume does not change.)

P17-003.label: Owner earnings: full concluding discussion and qualifications · berkshire-letter-1986:u0287
P17-003.context_title: Owner earnings: full concluding discussion and qualifications
P17-003.date_basis: Signature date recorded in the reviewed original-source dossier; report year is separate.

paragraphs.speaker: Warren Buffett
paragraphs.speaker_basis: Signed shareholder-letter authorship; embedded quotations retain their original introduction.

P17-003.excerpt: Our owner-earnings equation does not yield the deceptively precise figures provided by GAAP, since( c) must be a guess - and one sometimes very difficult to make. Despite this problem, we consider the owner earnings figure, not the GAAP figure, to be the relevant item for valuation purposes - both for investors in buying stocks and for managers in buying entire businesses. We agree with Keynes's observation: "I would rather be vaguely right than precisely wrong."

P17-007.label: Owner earnings: full concluding discussion and qualifications · berkshire-letter-1986:u0291
P17-007.context_title: Owner earnings: full concluding discussion and qualifications
P17-007.date_basis: Signature date recorded in the reviewed original-source dossier; report year is separate.

paragraphs.speaker: Warren Buffett
paragraphs.speaker_basis: Signed shareholder-letter authorship; embedded quotations retain their original introduction.

P17-007.excerpt: All of this points up the absurdity of the "cash flow" numbers that are often set forth in Wall Street reports. These numbers routinely include (a) plus (b) - but do not subtract ( c) . Most sales brochures of investment bankers also feature deceptive presentations of this kind. These imply that the business being offered is the commercial counterpart of the Pyramids - forever state-of-the-art, never needing to be replaced, improved or refurbished. Indeed, if all U.S. corporations were to be offered simultaneously for sale through our leading investment bankers - and if the sales brochures describing them were to be believed - governmental projections of national plant and equipment spending would have to be slashed by 90%.

P17-008.label: Owner earnings: full concluding discussion and qualifications · berkshire-letter-1986:u0292
P17-008.context_title: Owner earnings: full concluding discussion and qualifications
P17-008.date_basis: Signature date recorded in the reviewed original-source dossier; report year is separate.

paragraphs.speaker: Warren Buffett
paragraphs.speaker_basis: Signed shareholder-letter authorship; embedded quotations retain their original introduction.

P17-008.excerpt: "Cash Flow", true, may serve as a shorthand of some utility in descriptions of certain real estate businesses or other enterprises that make huge initial outlays and only tiny outlays thereafter. A company whose only holding is a bridge or an extremely long-lived gas field would be an example. But "cash flow" is meaningless in such businesses as manufacturing, retailing, extractive companies, and utilities because, for them, ( c) is always significant. To be sure, businesses of this kind may in a given year be able to defer capital spending. But over a five- or ten-year period, they must make the investment - or the business decays.

P01-003.label: Valuation, knowability and margin of safety · berkshire-letter-1992:u0076
P01-003.context_title: Valuation, knowability and margin of safety

paragraphs.speaker: Warren Buffett
paragraphs.speaker_basis: Signed shareholder-letter authorship; embedded quotations retain their original introduction.

P01-003.excerpt: We view that as fuzzy thinking (in which, it must be confessed, I myself engaged some years ago). In our opinion, the two approaches are joined at the hip: Growth is always a component in the calculation of value, constituting a variable whose importance can range from negligible to enormous and whose impact can be negative as well as positive.

P01-007.label: Valuation, knowability and margin of safety · berkshire-letter-1992:u0080
P01-007.context_title: Valuation, knowability and margin of safety

paragraphs.speaker: Warren Buffett
paragraphs.speaker_basis: Signed shareholder-letter authorship; embedded quotations retain their original introduction.

P01-007.excerpt: Growth benefits investors only when the business in point can invest at incremental returns that are enticing - in other words, only when each dollar used to finance the growth creates over a dollar of long-term market value. In the case of a low-return business requiring incremental funds, growth hurts the investor.

P01-010.label: Valuation, knowability and margin of safety · berkshire-letter-1992:u0083
P01-010.context_title: Valuation, knowability and margin of safety

paragraphs.speaker: Warren Buffett
paragraphs.speaker_basis: Signed shareholder-letter authorship; embedded quotations retain their original introduction.

P01-010.excerpt: Leaving the question of price aside, the best business to own is one that over an extended period can employ large amounts of incremental capital at very high rates of return. The worst business to own is one that must, or will, do the opposite - that is, consistently employ ever-greater amounts of capital at very low rates of return. Unfortunately, the first type of business is very hard to find: Most high-return businesses need relatively little capital. Shareholders of such a business usually will benefit if it pays out most of its earnings in dividends or makes significant stock repurchases.

P19-004.label: Franchise economics: complete first argument before the printed separator · berkshire-letter-1991:u0034
P19-004.context_title: Franchise economics: complete first argument before the printed separator
P19-004.date_basis: Original signed closing paragraph; report year is separate.

paragraphs.speaker: Warren Buffett
paragraphs.speaker_basis: Signed shareholder-letter authorship; embedded quotations retain their original introduction.

P19-004.excerpt: An economic franchise arises from a product or service that: (1) is needed or desired; (2) is thought by its customers to have no close substitute and; (3) is not subject to price regulation. The existence of all three conditions will be demonstrated by a company's ability to regularly price its product or service aggressively and thereby to earn high rates of return on capital. Moreover, franchises can tolerate mis-management. Inept managers may diminish a franchise's profitability, but they cannot inflict mortal damage.

P19-005.label: Franchise economics: complete first argument before the printed separator · berkshire-letter-1991:u0035
P19-005.context_title: Franchise economics: complete first argument before the printed separator
P19-005.date_basis: Original signed closing paragraph; report year is separate.

paragraphs.speaker: Warren Buffett
paragraphs.speaker_basis: Signed shareholder-letter authorship; embedded quotations retain their original introduction.

P19-005.excerpt: In contrast, "a business" earns exceptional profits only if it is the low-cost operator or if supply of its product or service is tight. Tightness in supply usually does not last long. With superior management, a company may maintain its status as a low- cost operator for a much longer time, but even then unceasingly faces the possibility of competitive attack. And a business, unlike a franchise, can be killed by poor management.

P19-003.label: Franchise economics: complete first argument before the printed separator · berkshire-letter-1991:u0033
P19-003.context_title: Franchise economics: complete first argument before the printed separator
P19-003.date_basis: Original signed closing paragraph; report year is separate.

paragraphs.speaker: Warren Buffett
paragraphs.speaker_basis: Signed shareholder-letter authorship; embedded quotations retain their original introduction.

P19-003.excerpt: The fact is that newspaper, television, and magazine properties have begun to resemble businesses more than franchises in their economic behavior. Let's take a quick look at the characteristics separating these two classes of enterprise, keeping in mind, however, that many operations fall in some middle ground and can best be described as weak franchises or strong businesses.

P16-003.label: Twenty Years in a Candy Store · berkshire-letter-1991:u0047
P16-003.context_title: Twenty Years in a Candy Store
P16-003.date_basis: Original signed closing paragraph; report year is separate.

paragraphs.speaker: Warren Buffett
paragraphs.speaker_basis: Signed shareholder-letter authorship; embedded quotations retain their original introduction.

P16-003.excerpt: The sales of trading stamps by Blue Chip thereafter declined from $102.5 million in 1972 to $1.2 million in 1991. But See's candy sales in the same period increased from $29 million to $196 million. Moreover, profits at See's grew even faster than sales, from $4.2 million pre-tax in 1972 to $42.4 million last year.

P16-004.label: Twenty Years in a Candy Store · berkshire-letter-1991:u0048
P16-004.context_title: Twenty Years in a Candy Store
P16-004.date_basis: Original signed closing paragraph; report year is separate.

paragraphs.speaker: Warren Buffett
paragraphs.speaker_basis: Signed shareholder-letter authorship; embedded quotations retain their original introduction.

P16-004.excerpt: For an increase in profits to be evaluated properly, it must be compared with the incremental capital investment required to produce it. On this score, See's has been astounding: The company now operates comfortably with only $25 million of net worth, which means that our beginning base of $7 million has had to be supplemented by only $18 million of reinvested earnings. Meanwhile, See's remaining pre-tax profits of $410 million were distributed to Blue Chip/Berkshire during the 20 years for these companies to deploy (after payment of taxes) in whatever way made most sense.

P01-011.label: Valuation, knowability and margin of safety · berkshire-letter-1992:u0084
P01-011.context_title: Valuation, knowability and margin of safety

paragraphs.speaker: Warren Buffett
paragraphs.speaker_basis: Signed shareholder-letter authorship; embedded quotations retain their original introduction.

P01-011.excerpt: Though the mathematical calculations required to evaluate equities are not difficult, an analyst - even one who is experienced and intelligent - can easily go wrong in estimating future "coupons." At Berkshire, we attempt to deal with this problem in two ways. First, we try to stick to businesses we believe we understand. That means they must be relatively simple and stable in character. If a business is complex or subject to constant change, we're not smart enough to predict future cash flows. Incidentally, that shortcoming doesn't bother us. What counts for most people in investing is not how much they know, but rather how realistically they define what they don't know. An investor needs to do very few things right as long as he or she avoids big mistakes.

P01-012.label: Valuation, knowability and margin of safety · berkshire-letter-1992:u0085
P01-012.context_title: Valuation, knowability and margin of safety

paragraphs.speaker: Warren Buffett
paragraphs.speaker_basis: Signed shareholder-letter authorship; embedded quotations retain their original introduction.

P01-012.excerpt: Second, and equally important, we insist on a margin of safety in our purchase price. If we calculate the value of a common stock to be only slightly higher than its price, we're not interested in buying. We believe this margin-of-safety principle, so strongly emphasized by Ben Graham, to be the cornerstone of investment success.

data.question: How does required working capital affect owner earnings?

answer.title: Required working capital reduces owner earnings through component (c)
answer.lead: In Buffett's owner earnings formula, if a business requires additional working capital to maintain its competitive position and unit volume, that increment is included in component (c), which is subtracted from the sum of reported earnings plus non-cash charges. In other words, working capital needs that are necessary just to hold ground competitively reduce the cash truly available to owners, just as capitalized expenditures for plant and equipment do. [[P17-002]]
sections: The formula and the LIFO exception

Owner earnings are defined as (a) reported earnings plus (b) depreciation, depletion, amortization, and certain other non-cash charges, less (c) the average annual amount of capitalized expenditures for plant and equipment and similar items that the business requires to fully maintain its long-term competitive position and unit volume. Buffett adds the explicit qualification: if the business requires additional working capital to maintain its competitive position and unit volume, the increment also should be included in (c). He then notes an important exception: businesses following the LIFO inventory method usually do not require additional working capital if unit volume does not change. [[P17-002]]

This means that for non-LIFO businesses with growing unit volumes or rising input costs, the working capital drain is a real reduction in owner earnings, even though it may not appear as an expense on the income statement. For LIFO businesses with stable volumes, this particular drag is generally absent. [[P17-002]]

Buffett acknowledges that (c) must be a guess and is sometimes very difficult to estimate, yet he still considers the owner earnings figure, not the GAAP figure, to be the relevant item for valuation purposes for both investors buying stocks and managers buying entire businesses. He quotes Keynes: he would rather be vaguely right than precisely wrong. [[P17-003]]

The broader principle is that a business requiring more and more reinvestment just to maintain its position produces less cash for owners over time. Buffett has also stated that the best business is one that gives you more and more money every year without putting up anything to get it, or very little, while the worst is one forced to reinvest at low returns just to stay in the game. [[P12-007]][[P12-009]]

When evaluating a company's true earning power for owners, one must ask whether unit volume growth or inflation is pulling additional working capital into the business on a permanent basis. If so, that capital is not free cash flow and must be deducted from the owner earnings figure, reducing the amount available for dividends, buybacks, or further reinvestment at attractive rates. [[P17-002]][[P17-003]]
